newsitem.title: UK: Courtaulds Textiles says better '97 in view.
newsitem.headline: Courtaulds Textiles says better '97 in view.

text.p: Courtaulds Textiles Plc said on Thursday it had taken "an encouraging first step towards delivering better results in 1997."
The group reported 1996 pre-tax profit of just 400,000 stg compared with 36.5 million stg in 1995 after taking an expected restructuring charge of 31.7 million stg.

Chief executive Colin Dyer said in a statement that "decisive actions produced an improved result in the second half, with pre-execptional profit before tax slightly ahead of that achieved in the second year."
Dyer said the reorganisation was "proceeding ahead of plan," with eight businesses sold since June 1996.
The group's "immediate objective is to build profit towards 1995 levels as the first important stage towards achieving our targeted 17 percent return on average capital employed."

Dyer said trading so far in 1997 "had continued the pattern of last year's second half with encouraging progress, particularly in the UK and USA," adding that "at this early stage of the year we are meeting our targets." The group said its decision to hold its dividend at 15.3 pence reflected confidence "in the prospects of the business."
Before exceptional items pre-tax profit fell to 32.1 million stg from 40.4 million stg, largely due to profit falls in U.S. lace and stretch fabrics in the first half of the year, it said.
Gearing declined to 19 percent at the end of 1996 from 37 percent a year before.

Operating profits in the UK advanced 31 percent before exceptionals, Courtaulds Textiles said, although this was "more than offset by the effects of tough trading conditions in the USA and Continental Europe."
The company said trade with its largest customer, British clothes and foods retailer Marks & Spencer Plc "progressed healthily" with total sales up eight percent to 306 million stg.
Courtaulds Textiles said it expected its restructuring to result in annual cost savings of between 10 and 13 million stg by 1998.
Shares in the company were up 3 1/2 pence to 267 1/2 pence in midmorning trading.
